narrative:
Based on the assessment, there is a 55% chance you will fail your final year, which exceeds the 10% threshold that requires you to take remedial courses. While this may feel discouraging, understanding what is driving this prediction can help you take meaningful action.

The single most influential factor pushing toward this prediction is that you have experienced one past class failure. Among students who are not required to take remedial courses, the average number of past failures is zero, meaning your academic history stands out as a significant concern and is the strongest signal the model identified.

Your family size is the second most important factor, and here it actually works in your favor. Coming from a smaller household is associated with a slightly lower risk of failing, nudging the prediction in a positive direction.

The third key factor is your weekly study time, which is currently less than two hours. This pushes the prediction back toward failing. Among students not required to take remedial courses, the majority study between two and ten hours per week, so your current study habits fall noticeably short of what tends to support academic success.

The good news is that two of these three factors are within your control. You cannot change your past, but you can significantly change how much time you dedicate to studying each week. Increasing your study hours to at least two to five hours per week would bring you in line with your more successful peers.

Engaging fully with the remedial courses offered to you is the most important next step you can take right now.
